recentes.titreEditorial: Your agents also serve those attacking you
The assistant that wrote now acts
AI on the phone, debt on the books
AI reaches the UN Security Council
Anthropic and OpenAI ship on the same day

More than twenty countries call for stronger human oversight of AI, without the United States, China or France, while Washington and Beijing open a warning channel between them ahead of the Trump-Xi summit. Google launches its Googlebook at $899 to sell Gemini, Meta's Muse agent races to the top of the charts before being blocked by Amazon and flagged for a security flaw, and British Columbia sues OpenAI after a mass shooting.

Charles III gathers AI bosses in Scotland and warns of \"existential dangers\", while a Pew survey across 37 countries shows a worldwide fear of job destruction. Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act, Mistral moves into Firefox, Nvidia, Google and Anthropic join forces to find 100 gigawatts on the power grid, and Huawei pulls its next training chip forward by nine months to close the gap with Nvidia.

OpenAI admits six model misbehaviours and publishes a framework to report them, the same day Google opens the connected home to agents and Anthropic folds its interfaces into a single Claude that decides for itself how much work to take on. The agent moves from reading to acting. Meanwhile Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act to keep minors off social media, Mistral arrives in Firefox, and Huawei pulls its next AI chip nine months forward to cut China's dependence on Nvidia.
Silicon Valley refuses to brake, Washington splits
AI leaders' call to slow down splits the world

AI leaders call for slowing the race, the White House refuses: Dario Amodei argues for \"pacing the frontier\", Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis agree, Donald Trump replies that he will not hand his lead to China, and Asian markets fall. Anthropic is eyeing the Nasdaq for a listing that could exceed $86 billion while OpenAI backs away from its own, SoftBank borrows $11.9 billion to fund OpenAI and Christine Lagarde warns about the financial cost of AI. In China, Z.ai returns to raise $5 billion in Hong Kong and the intelligence chief warns about the risks of AI.

AI safety moves from the activist fringe to mainstream debate: Sam Altman says he is ready to slow frontier AI development and is testing whether such a brake would be legal, a former Anthropic researcher warns that \"AI could kill us all,\" OpenAI adds a worried researcher to its board, and Anthropic publishes 161 pages of Claude misuse, from Yemeni missiles to fake dating profiles. In Europe, the CNIL sets rules for electronic invoicing and the EU's cybersecurity agency trials Anthropic's most offensive model. In China, DeepSeek reignites the price war with its V4.1 Flash model and chipmaker Enflame jumps 188% on its stock market debut. Microsoft plans 38 gigawatts of data centres and Jensen Huang promises Nvidia 70% growth.
Apple's first Ternus keynote and the OECD's student warning
OpenAI claims a Navier-Stokes proof, then a credit fight erupts

Mistral AI raises €3 billion at a €21 billion valuation in a round led by Samsung; the labor-law scholar Jean-Emmanuel Ray reminds employers that the AI Act requires them to inventory their high-risk AI systems and inform staff by the end of 2027, while BPCE stands up its AI Factory and Bercy renegotiates the French state's IT contracts; China targets 9,800 eflops of compute and Huawei launches its first stacked-circuit chip; Revolut completes the first AI-initiated payment in France

Moody's finds that Chinese companies get more compute per dollar spent than the US giants; the Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft over copyright while the split of the Anthropic settlement pits authors against publishers; Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, describes an alien mind and calls for guardrails; and US job seekers hide instructions in their resumes to trick recruiters' AI
OpenAI ships GPT-6 Astra as three assistants go dark
Washington backs OpenAI against the New York Times
OpenAI rates Astra at critical cyber capability

The European Commission ranks ChatGPT among its most closely watched services under the DSA, the first generative AI targeted, OpenAI moves some of its large customers to performance-based billing, Anthropic signs $35 billion in compute with Lambda ahead of its IPO, and Nvidia invests $3.5 billion in MediaTek to stay indispensable

Sony Music and Warner sue Anthropic for \"one of the largest thefts of intellectual property in history\" on the eve of its stock market listing, Bill Gates calls for taxing machines, Google rolls out its AI answers by default at the expense of the blue links, and Caterpillar applies thirty years of mining automation to AI

Nvidia moves on Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, the open-source platform founded by three French entrepreneurs, the same week it was breached by OpenAI's agents; a federal judge overturns the Pentagon's ban on Anthropic, OpenAI brings advertising to ChatGPT in India, Zhipu unveils an open model trained on 100,000 Chinese chips, and OpenAI documents what critical thinking changes about using a chatbot

Nvidia posts a record $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue and looks ahead to 2028, while Amazon triples its chip order and Anthropic signs $45 billion of compute with Nscale; on the same day, OpenAI releases its report on the Hugging Face breach carried out by nearly 700 of its own agents, Bill Gates breaks his silence to call for a robot tax, and the CNIL updates its open-model traceability tool
Open-weight models pass proprietary ones on Vercel
Uber fined €825 million over automated decisions

Nvidia warns its biggest customers of a price rise above 15% on its AI servers as memory costs soar; the same day SoftBank places a record bond to fund OpenAI, Samsung returns $79 billion under the pressure of the AI boom, Alibaba raises $10.2 billion in Hong Kong, and Hugging Face is said to be exploring a sale at around $13 billion
Anthropic eyes a SpaceX-sized listing as enterprise buyers switch models
The AI Act makes provenance a job
OpenAI freezes part of Astra over cyber risk
Jeff Dean leaves Google as DeepMind reshuffles its command

edition.titreEditorial: Your agents also serve those attacking you
edition.chapeau: AMD buys World Labs, Fei-Fei Li's start-up, for $8.2 billion, Anthropic ships Claude Sonnet 5.5 and OpenAI holds back its Astra model on safety grounds. On the same day, a cloned lawyer's voice costs an Italian bank €95 million and agents steal 600,000 bank cards in a few hours: the attacker now has the same agents as your teams.

une.titre: AMD buys World Labs, Fei-Fei Li's start-up, for $8.2 billion
une.texteHtml: The American chipmaker announced on Monday 28 September the all-stock acquisition of World Labs, the spatial-AI lab founded in 2024 by Stanford researcher Fei-Fei Li, often called the "godmother of AI". Fei-Fei Li joins AMD as executive vice-president and chief scientist, and her team brings its expertise in world-generation models, systems that build three-dimensional environments from an image or a piece of text. World Labs, valued at a billion dollars just months after its birth, had launched a first commercial product this year. At $8.2 billion, the deal is the second largest in AMD's history after the Xilinx acquisition in 2022, and aims to challenge Nvidia on the turf of physical AI, the kind that drives robots and machines in the real world. Closing is expected by the end of the year.

items.titre: Mistral opens a Munich office to speed up its move to industrial scale
items.texteHtml: The French unicorn is setting up offices in Munich, close to Germany's industrial base, to bring its teams nearer to large manufacturing and automotive accounts. The geography states the strategy: after making its mark on open models and sovereignty, Mistral is looking for deployments in European industry, where the budgets and the heavyweight use cases are. The German base complements the Paris roots rather than replacing them.

items.titre: French Wikipedia now bans generative AI for writing its articles
items.texteHtml: The encyclopedia's community has moved the use of text-generation models from "strongly discouraged" to a general ban, with only two exceptions. The decision aims to protect the reliability of articles against the fabrications and plausible errors these tools produce, in an encyclopedia where every claim must point to a verifiable source. The move stands apart from the drive to embed AI everywhere else, and draws a clear line for one of the most visited sites in the world.

items.titre: An AI-cloned lawyer's voice costs an Italian bank €95 million
items.texteHtml: Fraudsters extracted €95 million from Fideuram, the private-banking arm of Intesa Sanpaolo, according to Numerama. The scheme combined two levers: impersonating the boss on WhatsApp, then a call in which a lawyer's voice, cloned by AI, approved the transfers. More than a third of the sum is still missing to date. The case shows that CEO fraud, a known technique, becomes formidable when the voice giving the order is one you think you recognise.

items.titre: Anthropic ships Claude Sonnet 5.5, faster and cheaper
items.texteHtml: The American company unveiled on Monday 28 September the new version of its mid-range model, presented as a work partner "significantly cheaper and faster". Sonnet 5.5 runs more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and costs up to 30% less per task, at an unchanged price per token (the unit of text that is billed). On Terminal-Bench 4.0, a coding test, it jumps from 10.3% to 70.6% and beats Opus 5.5, the company's high-end model. The market logic holds: the best performance-to-price ratio no longer comes from the heaviest model, but from a mid-range model sharpened for everyday tasks.

items.titre: OpenAI holds back its Astra model on the eve of its developer conference
items.texteHtml: The company has shelved the GPT-6.1 Astra version of its model, which scored worse on safety evaluations than the version already in service, Bloomberg reports. The new build did improve on the model's "laziness", its tendency not to finish a requested task. An executive told the Wall Street Journal that the model followed instructions poorly. The decision comes on the eve of OpenAI's developer conference, an event built to show off new releases, and extends a run of cautious moves after several safety incidents this summer. Holding back a more capable model because it fails safety tests remains rare in a sector chasing power.

items.titre: Nvidia launches an open platform to contain agents that go off the rails
items.texteHtml: Jensen Huang presented on Monday 28 September the Open Agent Safety Platform, a set of software and hardware that adds independent safety layers around AI agents. The tool, presented in response to a wave of incidents where agents breached the walls meant to contain them, promises to isolate within milliseconds an agent trying to step outside its perimeter, including during execution. Nvidia is betting on open code to make it a shared building block for the sector. The chip supplier that fed the wave of agents now also offers the harness to hold them.

items.titre: Bain estimates it will take $6 trillion in annual revenue to make AI data centres pay off
items.texteHtml: The firm Bain & Company puts at $6 trillion the annual revenue the AI industry will have to reach by 2031 to justify the capital sunk into building data centres. Productivity gains and consumer uses alone will not bring in enough, warns the report relayed by La Tribune: new markets will have to emerge to close the gap. The figure gives a measure of the bet: $6 trillion a year, more than the annual gross domestic product of Japan, the world's third-largest economy, to be found every year just to cover the infrastructure bill.

items.titre: ByteDance alone holds a fifth of China's data-centre capacity
items.texteHtml: The owner of TikTok accounts for about a fifth of the data-centre capacity already delivered in China, making it the country's biggest tenant and the main driver of its rise in AI, according to new estimates from the firm SemiAnalysis. The figure rests on tracking more than 1,000 facilities operated by more than 60 companies. ByteDance rents almost all of its fleet rather than owning it, and uses that power to feed its AI products, including the Doubao assistant. The concentration illustrates a Chinese model in which a few digital giants alone pull demand for compute.

items.titre: Samsung invests a billion dollars in AI data centres
items.texteHtml: Samsung Electronics and five of its subsidiaries are pouring a billion dollars in total into an American company run by a former Amazon Web Services executive and backed by the KKR fund, Bloomberg and Nikkei Asia report. The deal reinforces the South Korean group's push into the fast-growing AI-infrastructure market. A maker of memory and chips, Samsung is also positioning itself as an investor in the centres that will consume those components, securing an outlet for its production. South Korea intends to count in a race where compute is becoming the strategic asset.

items.titre: H Company releases Holo4, a family of models for agents that can use a computer
items.texteHtml: The French start-up H Company has posted Holo4 on Hugging Face, a series of models designed to drive "computer-use" agents, that is, able to manipulate an interface the way a human would, reading the screen and clicking. The open release, documented on the Hugging Face blog, puts a European player on the ground of autonomous agents now dominated by the big American labs. The bet deserves attention: an open agent model installed and run in-house avoids exposing an organisation's screens to a third-party service.

items.titre: Chinese chipmaker CanSemi's IPO oversubscribed more than 2,300 times
items.texteHtml: The retail tranche of the IPO of chipmaker CanSemi, based in Guangzhou, was oversubscribed more than 2,300 times, a sign of Chinese investors' appetite for silicon photonics and domestic AI infrastructure.

items.titre: Google fights the EU's attempt to open Android to rival AI
items.texteHtml: Brussels wants to force Google to open its Android system to rival AI assistants and to share search data with competing providers; the company is opposing the move, citing the risks to its ecosystem.

analyse.titre: The attacker now has the same agents as your teams: a cloned lawyer's voice costs Fideuram €95 million, agents steal 600,000 cards in a few hours and AI-written malware targets French bank accounts, which makes obsolete the security training that taught people to spot a clumsy email, and the concrete lever for a French organisation is to require out-of-band verification, a callback to a known number and two-person approval, for any movement of money or data above a threshold.
analyse.these: The same wave of agents that equips your teams equips those attacking you; a cloned voice slips past every reflex learned to spot a phishing email, so the move that protects a French organisation is to require out-of-band verification for any movement of money or sensitive data, and to redo a security training that the cloned voice has made obsolete.
analyse.html:
An AI-cloned lawyer's voice cost Fideuram, the private bank of Intesa Sanpaolo, €95 million, and more than a third of the sum is still missing. On the same day, Clubic reports that agents stole 600,000 bank card numbers in a few hours, a job that used to take a human ring weeks. Siècle Digital describes RemControl, malware written with the help of AI that targets bank accounts in France, Spain and Italy. And researchers were able to read, with no credentials at all, the contents of 16,326 databases, half of which held personal data, because code agents had put them online wide open.

These facts point in one direction, and it aims at the heart of your organisation. The wave of agents you are evaluating for your teams equips, in exactly the same way, those attacking you. The barrier falls on both sides of the wall at once.

This shift makes a whole part of your security training obsolete. We have spent ten years teaching staff to spot the clumsy email: the spelling mistake, the dodgy address, the unexpected attachment. A familiar voice calling on WhatsApp slips past all those reflexes. Fideuram's accountant did not click a link, they trusted a voice.

The skill that gains value then changes in nature. It now rests on verification outside the channel carrying the request, once sniffing out the fake becomes impossible the moment the copy is perfect. Set a simple rule, written down, known to everyone: above a threshold, any movement of money or sensitive data requires a callback to an already-registered number and approval by two people, whatever the voice that gave the order. The rule applies to the executive assistant as much as to the chief financial officer, because the fraud targets the person who executes, not the firewall.

Fideuram's firewall held. It was a human who picked up the phone. The weak point of your security in 2026 lies in the reflex of trust that forty years of the telephone have ingrained, the one that gets an order approved because the voice is recognised. No software update fixes it. Only training does.

The Masteria editorial team.
